title: Workflows, agents and who owns the control flow

items.stem: What is the clearest difference between a workflow and an agent in how they run?

options.text: Workflows never call a language model, while agents always do
Code sets the order of steps in a workflow; the model does in an agent
Agents can call tools, while workflows only return fixed text answers
Agents are always more accurate, while workflows are always cheaper

items.stem: Your code always runs check_calendar, then one model call picks the best free slot from the list, then code books it. Who owns the control flow, meaning who decides which step comes next?

options.text: The model, because it makes the key choice in the process
The tool, because its result decides what happens next
The code, because it fixes the order and the model fills one step
The model and the code, because each one runs some steps

items.stem: Your code always runs search_manuals, then one model call writes the answer. A student asks, "Is the laser cutter free on Friday?" What happens?

options.text: It still searches the manuals first, because the code fixes that path
The model sees a booking question and adds a calendar check step
The model skips the search and answers the question from training
The workflow stops and asks the student to rephrase the question

items.stem: A fixed workflow uses 2 model calls per request; an agent averages 5, and every call costs the same. For 300 requests, how many more model calls does the agent use?
Which request is the best fit for an agent rather than a fixed workflow?

options.text: Look up a machine's opening hours from a fixed table
Book the slot a student picked and email a confirmation
Find out why a student's prints keep failing, using the manuals
Reformat each day's bookings as a line in a weekly report

items.stem: A teammate wants booking (check the calendar, book the slot, send a confirmation) to run as an agent. In one sentence, why might a fixed workflow be better there?
